uncertainties: This is a career profile, not a 1996 snapshot. Privacy arguments date from 2010, assisted-dying opposition from 2017, nuclear-power opposition from 2024, and latest migration, taxation and AUKUS statements from 2026.
His 1995–1996 refusal to override Northern Territory euthanasia legislation concerned constitutional responsibility; it does not contradict his later personal opposition to assisted dying.

Moral reservations about abortion are cautiously inferred from the ABC expert assessment of his Catholic outlook, not attributed as a newly verified personal statement or a proposal to ban all abortions. Same-sex marriage, adoption and current gender identity questions remain neutral where evidence is insufficient.
Sexual-conduct privacy legislation is not evidence for unrestricted drug legalisation, prostitution policy or every modern family-law position.

The foreign-policy profile retains both government peacekeeping/security cooperation and later opposition to AUKUS. His statements about possible US deployments and military outcomes are opinions, not independently established facts.
Nuclear-energy opposition is supported by his explicit 2024 statement, not inferred from opposition to nuclear submarines or weapons.

Cryptocurrency, facial recognition, mandatory vaccination, genetic enhancement, implants and cultured meat involve bounded inference or neutral answers; the questionnaire was never completed by Keating.
CBA privatisation began under Hawke and concluded under Howard; the profile attributes only Keating-era tranches and support for the programme to Keating.
The 2010 city speech contains an apparent reference to being Treasurer in the mid-1990s; the profile uses the independently verified 1983–1991 tenure.
distinctions: Unlike a generic socialist profile, he supported private ownership, financial deregulation and tariff reductions.
Unlike a laissez-faire liberal, he defended Medicare, compulsory superannuation, progressive taxation and public infrastructure.
Unlike Hawke, his later documented positions oppose voluntary assisted dying and domestic nuclear power while placing greater emphasis on avoiding US-led strategic confrontation with China.
Unlike a purely nationalist or isolationist profile, he supported multiculturalism, Asian economic integration and international peacekeeping.

similarityReview.reason: Shared democratic, pluralist and socially protective institutions explain the overlap. Keating differs from the existing Mattarella vector on economia (53.2 vs 62.5) and comercio (17.5 vs 30.0), reflecting documented privatisation, financial liberalisation and APEC trade integration. His civil-liberties emphasis yields poder 47.2 versus 58.8. These comparisons describe model outputs, not objectively measured historical distances; no answers were altered to manufacture separation.

Market reform and parliamentary democracy explain substantial overlap. The Keating career profile incorporates his later opposition to AUKUS and a Taiwan war, giving diplomacia 27.6 and intervencao 49.4 versus the existing Clinton model at 43.8 and 35.0. Compulsory superannuation, Medicare and Christian social ethics also remain explicit. This is a source-based distinction between editorial simulations, not a claim of measured historical distance. Answers were retained unchanged after review.

Both editorial profiles support democratic government, social protection and market reform. Keating’s financial liberalisation, privatisation and Asian trade integration give comercio 17.5 versus Carter’s 31.8. His compact-city and industrial-development record differs from Carter’s rural/conservation emphasis (tecnologia 52.4 versus 45.2). His later strategic autonomy positions also differ on intervencao (49.4 versus 41.0). This accepts documented political proximity between distinct people; archived answers are unchanged.
